prompt:
Solve the following problem as completely as you can.

<problem>
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ satisfy $A+A=\mathbb N_0$, and let $\sigma_A(n)=|\{(a,a')\in A^2: a\le a',\ a+a'=n\}|$. Since $A+A=\mathbb N_0$, one has $\sigma_A(n)\ge1$ for every $n$, and a counting argument gives $\sigma_A(n)\ge1$ on average at least of order $1$ (indeed $|A\cap[n]|\gg\sqrt n$). Does there exist an explicit (e.g. computable in polynomial time in $\log n$ for membership) set $A$ with $A+A=\mathbb N_0$ and $\sigma_A(n)\le C\log n$ for all $n\ge2$, with $C$ absolute? Weaker: is $\sigma_A(n)\le(\log n)^{C}$ achievable explicitly, improving the bound $n^{c/\log\log n}$?
</problem>

</finite_instance>

structured_output.text: I did not solve this. Known context: counting gives |A∩[n]| ≫ √n; Erdős (1956) proved non-constructively (probabilistically) that σ_A(n) ≍ log n is attainable. Explicit digit-based constructions (e.g. A = numbers with binary digits only in even positions ∪ only in odd positions) give A+A=N_0 but σ_A(n) can be n^c, because collisions in A_0+A_0 occur in families of size 2^{#digits}; refining with more blocks/mixed radices lowers this to n^{c/loglog n}, the bound quoted in the problem. I found no explicit construction achieving (log n)^C or C log n, nor a derandomization of Erdős's argument. Both questions remain open as far as I can tell.
